abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Valemetostat is an EZH2/1 inhibitor that has been approved in Japan for the treatment of patients with relapsed/refractory adult T‐cell leukemia/lymphoma, based mainly on results from a single‐arm phase II trial. It is currently under investigation worldwide for the treatment of other non‐Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs), including peripheral T‐cell lymphoma, and for solid tumors. Semi‐mechanistic population pharmacokinetic modeling of total and unbound valemetostat and an analysis of the platelet time course during treatment with valemetostat were conducted using data from five clinical trials (two in patients with NHL and three in healthy volunteers). Pharmacokinetic data, including 3162 total/1871 unbound valemetostat observations from 102 patients and 72 healthy volunteers, were described by a three‐compartment model with sequential zero‐/first‐order absorption and saturable binding in the central compartment. Alpha‐1‐acid glycoprotein (AAG) was the most influential covariate for total valemetostat exposure, yet had little impact on unbound exposure, meaning no dose adjustment was warranted based on AAG levels. The longitudinal platelet data from 101 patients (2313 observations) were adequately described by a modified Friberg model with two proliferation compartments, which characterized unique spontaneous recovery of platelet counts without dose modifications. A model‐based simulation quantitatively assessed the proposed dose‐adjustment guidance in case of platelet count decreased by comparing the probability of treatment discontinuation due to platelet count decreased with or without the dose adjustment. In summary, the models described observed total and unbound valemetostat concentrations and a unique time course of platelets during treatment, which can justify the clinical dose and provide dose‐adjustment guidance.

p.bold: WHAT IS THE CURRENT KNOWLEDGE ON THE TOPIC?

boxed-text.p:
Total valemetostat pharmacokinetics shows high interindividual variability in patients and may necessitate dose adjustment in certain subpopulations, with alpha‐1‐acid glycoprotein as a possible influential covariate. Platelet count decrease is the most common adverse event in patients and may necessitate dose modifications upon occurrence.
WHAT QUESTION DID THIS STUDY ADDRESS?

What is the pharmacokinetics of total and unbound valemetostat and of platelet dynamics during treatment like? Is initial valemetostat dose adjustment required for subpopulations considering high variability in exposure? How can the risk of platelet count decrease be mitigated?
WHAT DOES THIS STUDY ADD TO OUR KNOWLEDGE?

Semi‐mechanistic models for both total and unbound valemetostat pharmacokinetics and platelet dynamics were developed. The effects of covariates on pharmacokinetics and platelet dynamics were quantitatively described. The risk of treatment discontinuation due to platelet count decreased events was assessed.
HOW MIGHT THIS CHANGE DRUG DISCOVERY, DEVELOPMENT, AND/OR THERAPEUTICS?
The analyses support no initial dose adjustment in any subpopulations and the proposed guidance on dose adjustment due to platelet count decreased events.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Valemetostat tosylate (valemetostat; DS‐3201b) is an oral, potent, and selective dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog (EZH)2 and EZH1 under investigation for the treatment of various EZH2‐expressing cancers. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 EZH2 and EZH1 play a role in tumorigenesis and survival, with overexpression or gain‐of‐function mutation of EZH involved in the progression of many non‐Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs), including adult T‐cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL). 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10

Valemetostat is currently approved in Japan for the treatment of patients with relapsed or refractory (R/R) ATLL, at an approved standard dose of 200 mg once daily. 11 Regulatory approval was based mainly on positive results from the single‐arm phase II DS3201‐A‐J201 (“J201”; NCT04102150) trial in patients with R/R ATLL, which showed an overall response rate (ORR) of 48% (90% confidence interval [CI], 30.5–65.9), including 5 complete remissions and 7 partial remissions. 3 Valemetostat is also in clinical development worldwide for the treatment of other hematologic malignancies and solid tumors. 1 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 12 , 13

In vitro studies showed nonlinear binding of valemetostat in human plasma, with 96.6%, 94.2%, and 78.0% bound for 0.5, 3, and 10 μg/mL valemetostat, respectively. The protein binding ratio of valemetostat (0.6–10 μg/mL) was 56.0% to 92.3% in 0.1% alpha‐1‐acid glycoprotein (AAG), and 35.0% to 38.7% in 4% human serum albumin, suggesting that valemetostat mainly binds to AAG (data on file).

Previous pharmacokinetics (PK) assessment demonstrated higher mean maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) and mean area under the plasma concentration–time curve (AUC) of total valemetostat in patients with ATLL, as well as higher interindividual variability (IIV) of total valemetostat exposure than with healthy volunteers (HVs), upon administration of the same dose level.

In patients with ATLL enrolled in the J201 trial receiving valemetostat 200 mg once daily, mean (standard deviation, [SD]) Cmax was 2230 (1880) ng/mL for total valemetostat and 81.7 (56.4) ng/mL for unbound valemetostat, with mean (SD) AUC from time 0 to tau (24 h) (AUCtau) of 18,100 (17,500) ng·h/mL for total valemetostat and 499 (301) ng·h/mL for unbound valemetostat. 3 In HVs from two phase I trials, DS3201‐A‐J103 (“J103”; jRCT2080223748) and DS3201‐A‐J109 (“J109”; jRCT2071200043), which included PK assessment at a dose of 200 mg under fasted conditions, mean (SD) Cmax values ranged between 1340 (513) and 1520 (643) ng/mL for total valemetostat, with mean (SD) AUC up to the last quantifiable timepoint (AUClast) ranging between 10,100 (4270) and 10,600 (3690) ng·h/mL. Mean (SD) Cmax and mean (SD) AUClast for unbound valemetostat were 92.0 (41.2) ng/mL and 533 (220) ng·h/mL, respectively. 14 The higher concentration of AAG in the plasma of patients with ATLL than with HVs and the high affinity of valemetostat for AAG may be the causes of increased means and IIV. 15 , 16

In the phase I DS3201‐A‐J101 (J101; NCT02732275) and J201 valemetostat trials in patients with R/R NHL, platelet count decreased was the most common grade III or higher treatment‐emergent adverse event (TEAE) and it was reported as a dose‐limiting toxicity. 12 , 13 In these studies, the platelet time course during treatment showed unique dynamics, with an initial decline followed by a spontaneous partial recovery without dose interruptions and/or reductions. Therefore, clinical dose adjustments after platelet count decreases are not expected to be straightforward.

In the present study, the following pharmacometrics modeling was performed in order to support the standard dose, the necessity of an alternative dose for subpopulations, and dose adjustment guidance following platelet count decreased events. A population PK analysis: characterized the PK of both total and unbound valemetostat in HVs and patients with R/R NHL, including patients with ATLL; assessed the effect of covariates such as the binding protein, AAG; and explored subpopulations that may warrant an initial dose adjustment. Thereafter, a subsequent pharmacokinetic‐pharmacodynamic (PKPD) analysis described the unique platelet dynamics during valemetostat treatment in patients with R/R NHL using a semi‐mechanistic model and predicted that the risk of platelet count decreases by simulation to support the dose‐adjustment guidance.

sec.title: Study population
sec.p: This study utilized data from five clinical trials of valemetostat (Table S1): the phase I, multiple ascending‐dose J101 trial of valemetostat in patients with R/R NHLs 12 , 13 ; the phase I DS3201‐A‐J107 (“J107”, jRCT2080225242) drug–drug interaction (DDI) trial assessing the effect of multiple rifampicin doses on the PK of valemetostat in HVs 17 ; the phase I J109 study evaluating the effect of low‐fat meals on the PK of valemetostat in HVs 14 ; the phase II, multicenter, open‐label, single‐arm J201 study of valemetostat in patients with R/R ATLL 3 ; and the DS3201‐A‐U106 (“U106”, NCT04276662) single‐dose study assessing the PK of valemetostat in HVs with or without mild or moderate hepatic impairment. 18

sec.title: Population PK (PopPK) analyses
sec.p: The PopPK model included data from the five studies, excluding valemetostat PK data collected under fed conditions in the J109 food‐effect study or after receiving rifampicin in the J107 DDI study. Valemetostat plasma concentrations were determined using a validated liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) method with a lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) of 1 ng/mL for total concentration; LLOQ for unbound concentration is not applicable. 14

Both total and unbound valemetostat concentrations were modeled by a single PopPK model, which characterized both analytes simultaneously. Patients and HVs with at least one quantifiable valemetostat concentration were included in the PopPK analysis dataset. Valemetostat concentration data points without a clear and reliable dosing history, missing collection date or time, or missing any other critical information, were excluded from the analysis.
Data points below the limit of quantification (BLQ) were excluded from the model‐fitting steps of the analysis (M1 method) 19 considering the proportion was sufficiently low to avoid potential bias.

Considered covariates and their rationale for use are presented in Table S2. The median was used in place of a missing continuous covariate if ≤10% of values were missing, whereas regression‐based imputation methods were used if >10% were missing. Covariates were not considered for inclusion in primary model‐based analyses if >30% of values were missing.

sec.title: PopPK model development
sec.p: To model total and unbound concentrations simultaneously, a submodel allowing for linear or saturable binding of valemetostat in the central compartment was explored.
The absolute values of conditional weighted residuals (CWRES) 20 greater than five were assessed to identify potential outliers 21 ; but no concentrations were excluded.

IIV was described using an exponential error model, and residual variability was modeled with an additive error on the log scale. Differences in LC–MS/MS measurement methods for unbound valemetostat between the J101 trial and the other studies were accounted for with an estimated fixed effect to adjust unbound concentrations in J101, as well as additional study‐specific residual error variances.

The effects of body weight were described by an allometric model with a value of 0.75 for clearances and a value of 1 for volumes. The effects of the other continuous covariates were modeled using a power model, while the effects of categorical covariates were described by an exponential model as follows: Pri=eθr·∏l=1Mcovilreflβlr·∏l=M+1Lβlrcovil, where the typical value of a model parameter (P
ri ) is a function of L covariates, with l = 1, …, M representing the continuous covariates and l = M + 1, …, L representing the categorical binary covariates (covil) in the ith individual; θ
r represents the typical value of the rth parameter for a participant with reference covariate values; β lr represents the effect of covariate l on pharmacokinetic parameter r. A full covariate model was developed with measures to avoid correlation or collinearity in covariates; 22 continuous covariates with correlation coefficients >0.6 or with clear correlation with categorical covariates by graphical inspection were not simultaneously included.

Throughout the model development process, models were selected based on the performance evaluated for each of the intended purposes. 21 Evaluation included Akaike information criterion, standard goodness‐of‐fit plots, asymptotic standard errors for parameter estimates, shrinkage of interindividual and residual variability, prediction‐corrected visual predictive check (VPC), 23 and normalized prediction distribution errors (NPDEs). 24 , 25 , 26
The parameters for total and unbound valemetostat disposition including binding with AAG were simultaneously estimated with the first‐order conditional estimation with the ⴄ–ε interaction method.

sec.title: Applications
sec.p: For model‐based inference, forest plots demonstrating the effect of covariates on total and unbound valemetostat AUC for a dosing interval at steady state (AUCss), Cmax in the dosing interval at steady state (Cmax,ss), and minimum plasma concentration in the dosing interval at steady state (Cmin,ss) were generated from the PopPK model.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic‐pharmacodynamic (PKPD) analysis
sec.p: The model for platelet dynamics included all enrolled patients who met the following criteria: R/R NHL diagnosis, including ATLL; at least one valemetostat concentration observation in the PopPK analysis; and at least one platelet count during valemetostat treatment. Platelet counts on the day of or day after a transfusion were excluded from the analysis. The considered covariates are listed in Table S3. Covariate data imputation was handled in a similar way to the PopPK analyses.

sec.title: PKPD model development
sec.p: The PKPD modeling was conducted with the sequential approach (individual PK parameters method 27 ), and the structural part was developed as follows. An initial semi‐mechanistic model based on the Friberg model 28 employed unbound valemetostat to drive exposure‐related changes in platelets over time. The proliferation cell pool was divided into two compartments with different sensitivity to valemetostat, with or without an effect compartment, in order to describe the spontaneous partial recovery (Figure 1). NPDEs and CWRES were evaluated to help identify potential outliers with a threshold of five, 21 but no observations were excluded on this basis.

caption.p: Schematic representation of the population PKPD model. AAG, alpha‐1‐acid glycoprotein; CL, unbound valemetostat clearance; D1, duration of zero‐order input; EC50central and EC50effect, concentrations for 50% maximal inhibition; F1, bioavailability of zero‐order input; GAM1 and GAM2, sigmoidicity parameters for inhibitory valemetostat effects; GAMP, feedback parameter; KA, first‐order absorption rate constant; KD, binding affinity; KEL, platelet elimination rate constant; KEQ, equilibration rate constant; KPROL, proliferation rate constant; KTR, platelet transit rate constant; PKPD, pharmacokinetic‐pharmacodynamic; PROLIF, platelet proliferating compartments; RMAX, total binding capacity; Q3, Q4, intercompartmental clearances; V2, V3, V4, volumes of distribution.

sec.p: IIV was described using an exponential error model, and residual variability was modeled as a proportional error model. The effects of continuous and categorical covariates were modeled as in the PopPK analysis. Potential covariate effects were screened for all parameters with IIV included, however in the interest of model parsimony, only covariate effects on baseline were considered. The final choice of covariates was determined based on a combination of factors including correlation between predictors/parameter identifiability, model stability, and model diagnostics.

The model evaluation was performed similarly to the PopPK model, using standard goodness‐of‐fit plots, asymptotic standard errors after five iterations of importance sampling at the final estimates generated by the stochastic approximation expectation maximization (SAEM) step, and VPCs.
All model runs were estimated with the SAEM method.

sec.title: Applications
sec.p: Series of short‐ and adaptive long‐term dose simulations were employed to generate individual platelet dynamics, as well as PK profiles. Short‐term scenarios included simulations over two cycles (28 days in a cycle) of valemetostat at doses ranging from 100 to 300 mg; no dose‐adjustment protocol was implemented. Long‐term adaptive scenarios included a 200 mg starting dose with dose reduction/interruption in case of a grade IV platelet count decrease event (more details are provided in the Data S1).
All simulations were performed with N = 1000 replicate simulations of the patient population in the model estimation dataset (N = 102 subjects; N = 102,000 simulated patients overall per scenario).

sec.title: Software
sec.p: PopPK and PKPD analyses were conducted via nonlinear mixed‐effects modeling using a qualified installation of NONMEM®, version 7.5 (ICON Plc, Dublin, Ireland). Data assembly and all other pre‐ or post‐processing was conducted in R version 4.0. 29

sec.title: Ethics statement
sec.p: All studies were conducted in compliance with the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki, and Good Clinical Practice guidelines outlined by the International Council for Harmonization (ICH) and in accordance with applicable local regulatory requirements. The study protocols were approved by corresponding Institutional Review Boards, and all participants provided written informed consent prior to any trial procedure.

sec.title: Participant and sample disposition
sec.p: The PopPK analysis dataset included 174 participants that contributed 3162 total valemetostat observations. Of these, 3044 samples had quantifiable valemetostat concentrations (118 samples were BLQ). Of these participants, 172 participants contributed 1871 unbound valemetostat observations: 1705 samples had quantifiable unbound valemetostat concentrations and 166 samples were BLQ.

Demographic and clinical characteristics are given in Table 1. Most participants were Asian (122/174 [70.1%]) and were enrolled in Japan (119/174 [68.4%]). A high proportion of HVs were male (49/72 [68.1%]), whereas around half of the participants were male among the R/R NHL population (57/102 [55.9%]). A total of 43 participants (24.7%) had missing AAG values; for these, AAG levels were imputed using linear regression. No other covariates of interest had missing values.

sec.p: Total and unbound valemetostat concentrations peaked a~3–5 h after dosing and then declined steadily (Figure 2a).

caption.p: (a) Total (left) and unbound (right) plasma valemetostat concentrations over time after dose in a log scale; (b) Platelet percent change from baseline over time. Gray lines represent individual observations. Colored lines represent a smooth (univariate GAM) of the unbound valemetostat AUC at steady‐state tertiles. The black reference line (y = 0) represents no change from baseline. AUC, area under the concentration–time curve; GAM, generalized additive model.

sec.p: Higher total valemetostat concentrations were observed in patients with R/R NHL than with HVs; however, unbound valemetostat concentrations were similar between the two groups.

The final PKPD analysis dataset included 101 patients that contributed 2313 platelet observations, most (82.2%) of which were collected from the 71 Japanese patients. One patient had an unusually high platelet count that was consistently higher than any other observation in the population; this individual was excluded from the analysis. In addition, 129 platelet observations after transfusions were also excluded.

Platelet counts decreased in a valemetostat exposure–dependent manner. After an initial decline, platelet counts spontaneously recovered to a new steady state under continued daily dosing with valemetostat (Figure 2b).

sec.title: PopPK model development
sec.p: The final structure of the PopPK model for valemetostat consisted of a three‐compartment model with a sequential zero‐/first‐order absorption kinetic and a saturable binding component to model both total and unbound concentrations simultaneously. The binding compartment included estimable parameters for binding affinity (KD) and for total valemetostat concentration (total binding capacity [RMAX]) with an effect of AAG estimated on RMAX (Figure 1). 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 The estimated PopPK parameters are summarized in Table 2. The final covariate model included the effect of body weight on the apparent clearance (CL/F1) using the fixed allometric exponent of 0.75, and apparent and second apparent peripheral volumes of distribution (V3/F1 and V4/F1, respectively) using the fixed allometric exponent of 1. The model also included the effects of population (HV vs. patient), race (Asian vs. non‐Asian), sex (male vs. female), hepatic function (normal vs. mild vs. moderate impairment), and study (U106 vs. not U106) on CL/F1, and AAG on bioavailability (F1), CL/F1, and RMAX. The asymptotic 95% CIs for the covariate effects other than AAG included the null value (0 for continuous; 1 for categorical), indicating these were not statistically significant.

sec.p: The final model provided a reasonable description of the data, as judged by the goodness‐of‐fit and prediction‐corrected VPC plots (Figures S1–S3), with some possible underprediction around the peak particularly for total concentration.

sec.title: PopPK model applications
sec.p: The impact of covariates on total and unbound exposure is shown in Figure 3. Sex and race had a minimal impact on valemetostat exposure, whereas total and unbound steady‐state exposure decreased with weight and in HVs (compared with patients with NHL) and increased slightly in patients with hepatic impairment. Furthermore, AAG impacted total valemetostat exposure, but had little impact on unbound exposure.

The symbols indicate the median and the whiskers show the 95% CI for the simulated total and unbound AUCSS. Continuous covariates (weight and AAG) were evaluated at the 5th and 95th percentiles of the observed values in the entire model estimation dataset (including patients and healthy volunteers). sec.p: The impact of AAG on total and unbound valemetostat exposure was further assessed using post‐hoc PK parameters, as shown in Figure 4 although these results should be interpreted in light of 33.8% shrinkage on CL/F1 (Table 2). While total valemetostat exposure increased with increasing AAG, there was little variation in unbound exposure with AAG, suggesting that the high variation of total exposure is due to AAG (Figure 2a). In addition, the difference in AAG between HVs and patients contributed to the difference in total exposure through plasma protein binding (Figure 3).

sec.title: PKPD model development
sec.p: Potential covariate effects were screened for all parameters, but in the interest of model simplicity, only covariate effects on baseline were considered. The final covariates included were the effect of race (Asian vs. non‐Asian) and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) score (0 vs. ≥1).

The final model provided a reasonable description of the data, as judged by the goodness‐of‐fit and VPC plots, retaining slight deviation around the rebound (Day 100) and following a decrease of the observed platelets over time (Figures S4–S6).

Population parameters and the asymptotic 95% CIs were estimated (Table 2). The model showed that non‐Asian patients had baseline platelet estimates of approximately 91.3% (95% CI, 72.9–110) of that for an Asian patient. The 95% CIs for this estimate included the null value (1 for categorical), indicating this result was not statistically significant, and baseline platelets were comparable across Asian and non‐Asian patients. The effect of a baseline ECOG PS ≥1 on baseline platelets also had 95% CIs that included the null value (1.07; 95% CI, 0.84–1.29), indicating that baseline platelet values were comparable for patients with a baseline ECOG PS score of 0 and ≥1.

sec.title: PKPD model application
sec.p: Short‐term simulations of platelet dynamics for valemetostat doses of 100–300 mg showed that the incidence of grade III or grade IV platelet count decreased TEAEs (defined according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0) would increase at a higher daily dose level. Over the first two cycles, the proportion of treatment‐emergent grade III platelet count decreased events increased from 10.1% at 100 mg to 23.8% at 200 mg and 33.4% at 300 mg. Similarly, the proportion of grade IV platelet count decreased events increased from 2.5% at 100 mg to 11.0% at 200 mg and 21.4% at 300 mg (Table 3).

caption.p: Summary of results from the model‐based simulations.

tr.th: Percentage of patients with platelet count decreased events

fn.p: Simulations summarized as the percentage of patients experiencing 0–4 grade IV platelet count decreased events over 1 year. Simulated patients received 200 mg, which was reduced to 150 mg after the second Grade 4 event or 100 mg after the third Grade 4 event. Dosing was discontinued in patients experiencing four Grade 4 events. Grade 4 platelet count events were defined as a simulated platelet value that included residual error at clinical monitoring visits (every week over Cycle 1 and every 2 weeks thereafter).

sec.p: There was also a dose‐dependent decrease in the minimum simulated platelet and simulated platelet values at the end of the first or second cycle. Regardless of the dose, the median simulated time to platelet nadir over the first two cycles was 22 days.

Under long‐term simulations of adaptive dosing, 12.8% of simulated patients experienced more than one grade IV platelet count decrease event over the year. Among these patients, 31.9% experienced two episodes and 29.5% experienced three episodes of grade IV platelet count decreased and ~ 20% experienced either one or four episodes that required discontinuation.

In order to evaluate dose adjustment, a parallel simulation was performed with an identical setup, but without dose adjustment: platelets were monitored every 1 or 2 weeks, and doses held when grade IV platelet count decreased were observed (dosing was always restarted at 200 mg when recovery criteria were met). In this case, 66% of the simulated patients who experienced any grade IV platelet count decrease had four events which required discontinuation, while far fewer simulated patients had either two or three grade IV events when doses were not reduced. Finally, simulated patients with lower baseline platelet values experienced more grade IV platelet count decrease events compared with those with higher baseline platelet values.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: The present study developed a PopPK model of valemetostat that simultaneously described both total and unbound concentrations and quantitatively assessed the effect of covariates of interest. A semi‐mechanistic PKPD model for characterizing the unique platelet dynamics during valemetostat therapy was also developed. Both models were applied to evaluate the initial valemetostat dose and dose modifications after a platelet count decreased event.

The PopPK model consisted of a three‐compartment model with a sequential zero‐/first‐order absorption model, and an additional saturable binding component, which was linked to the central compartment. This mechanistically reasonable model adequately described observed concentrations of both total and unbound valemetostat concentrations.

During PopPK model development, several data‐related challenges needed to be addressed. AAG values were missing in some patients enrolled in J101. As baseline AAG was expected to be an important covariate in explaining PK variability, a multivariate regression model was developed to impute AAG values for patients in J101 with missing data. Most of the patients with imputed AAG were Asian (41 out of 43), and the imputed subset included more males and lower ECOG statuses in comparison with the rest of the patients (Table S4). While imputed AAG tended to be distributed around the median value in the patient population, these imputed values were not expected to be highly influential in estimating the effect of AAG on RMAX because the association with the EBE of the RMAX was consistent with that of non‐imputed AAG (Figure S7). Moreover, in the J101 trial, a different assay (ultracentrifugation) was used for unbound valemetostat measurements compared with all the other studies in the pooled analysis dataset (equilibrium dialysis); this could be the cause of the observed difference in unbound valemetostat concentrations between studies. To address this, a single fixed‐effect parameter was estimated to correct the derived unbound J101 concentrations so that they were consistent with the unbound concentration measurements from the other studies.

Considerable variability in total valemetostat exposure was observed in patients with NHL, and total concentrations were generally higher in patients with NHL compared with HVs. This difference could be explained by differences in plasma protein binding (ratio), as unbound valemetostat concentrations were similar between HVs and patients. As the impact on total exposure was high (ranging from a 0.51– to 1.41‐fold change in AUCss in patients with ATLL, Figure 3), valemetostat dose adjustment might be required depending on the exposure–response relationship when considering total exposure alone. In terms of covariate effects, the difference between HVs and patients with NHL was explained by unbound fraction and AAG levels. Protein binding had little impact on valemetostat unbound exposure. Therefore, these data suggest that AAG levels would not impact efficacy and safety. Other covariates, such as hepatic impairment, renal impairment, sex, body weight, and age had a minimal impact on exposure metrics and supported no dose adjustment in these subpopulations.

The platelet PKPD model included two proliferation compartments (representing the stem cells and the proliferating precursor cells in the bone marrow) with different sensitivities to valemetostat. This model adequately described observed platelet counts during valemetostat treatment, including spontaneous partial recovery without any dose reduction or treatment interruption. The platelet model included two covariates on baseline values: race (Asian vs. non‐Asian) and ECOG PS score (0 vs. ≥1).

The platelet count profile during continuous valemetostat dosing included a decline to the nadir after 22 days and then spontaneous recovery for all simulated doses (100–300 mg). This unique platelet profile was captured well by the developed model. Unusual platelet profiles have been previously reported with other agents. For example, in HER2‐positive metastatic breast cancer, administration of trastuzumab emtansine led to a steady and slow decline in platelets, with platelet levels not recovering during the treatment cycle. 34 This phenomenon was explained by separating the proliferation cell pool into a platelet proliferation lineage, which, when depleted, would lead to a new baseline derived from a platelet lineage with lower sensitivity to trastuzumab emtansine treatment. 34

In the simulated two‐cycle interval, there was a lower incidence of grade IV platelet count decreased events and smaller declines in platelet counts following lower valemetostat doses than with higher doses, suggesting that appropriate valemetostat dose modification could lead to lower drug exposure, attenuation of declining platelets over time, and subsequently fewer grade III or IV events. Long‐term simulations including instructions for dose modifications (Table S6) suggested that monitoring with dose reductions can reduce grade IV platelet count decreased events compared with the simulation with monitoring and no dose reduction. These simulations will help provide guidance for valemetostat dose adjustment in the case of grade IV platelet count decreased events, and eventually reduce the probability of treatment discontinuation due to this adverse event.

In summary, this study presents the development of a mechanistically reasonable model that describes the observed concentrations of both total and unbound valemetostat and a unique time course of platelets during treatment. Covariate analysis on valemetostat PK did not identify any subpopulations of patients who needed dose adjustment. A dosing regimen of valemetostat 200 mg with appropriate dose‐adjustment instructions can minimize grade IV platelet count decreased events during treatment. This model‐based approach provides support for the clinical dose of valemetostat in patients with ATLL and for dose‐adjustment guidance.
